An explainable AI helps experts attribute Rembrandt; what surgeons want from AI; the LLM radar.
TECH RADAR
An AI that helps art experts decide what Rembrandt really painted
No. 7 · Wednesday 28 October 2026 · LLMs and generative AI · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1In PNAS, a US–Colombian team presents an AI that helps attribute paintings to Rembrandt and shows which parts of the canvas drove its answer, so experts can check it.
2Asked which AI explanations they find useful, 47 neurosurgeons prefer a simple confidence score and a map of how sure the system is, over more elaborate techniques.
3LLM radar: research share has doubled in three years, and new GitHub projects on AI guardrails grew about 28 times in a year.

new papers on LLMs and generative AI today

research share of the vertical compared with 3 years ago
+2,712%
new GitHub projects on LLM guardrails, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences · 26 October · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Andrés Arias–Rosales and 4 others · Carnegie Mellon University, Universidad EAFIT, University of Maryland, College Park (United States, Colombia) · among the authors Jonathan Cagan, h-index 54
Context. Deciding whether a painting is by a great master or by a pupil can take experts decades of debate, and the answer changes a work's value and its place in history. AI can compare thousands of brushstrokes, but an answer without reasons is of little use to an art historian.
The team builds an 'explainable' AI that suggests an attribution and highlights the areas of the painting that weighed most in its judgement. It was trained on a dataset that deliberately includes artists close to the master, such as Rembrandt's pupils and teachers, and is calibrated to avoid overconfidence. It finds up to 97.9% of the works it should find and is right 95.8% of the time when it is highly confident. It is today's signal because it shows the role AI is taking in many fields: not replacing the expert, but giving arguments the expert can check.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · LLMS AND GENERATIVE AI
Explainable AIstrong growth
Research share +97% in 3 years · 4,475 papers in 2025
What it is about. Studies how to make an AI show why it gives a certain answer, so that people can judge whether to trust it. It matters most where mistakes are costly: medicine, finance, justice.
Exploring clinician interpretability of AI decision support systems for surgical anatomy recognition
Scientific Reports · 24 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Danyal Zaman Khan and 57 others · National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, University College London (United Kingdom and 10 other countries) · among the authors Danail V. Stoyanov, h-index 68
CONTEXTDuring keyhole brain surgery, an AI can outline anatomical structures on the camera image. But how should it show how reliable that outline is?
WHAT THEY DOThey asked 47 neurosurgeons from several countries to rank five ways of explaining the AI's output, using pituitary gland surgery as an example.
RESULTSurgeons consistently preferred methods based on certainty, a confidence score and a map of how sure the AI is at each boundary; heat maps and 'similar cases' were seen as more useful for teaching.
WHY IT MATTERSIt tells AI designers that doctors want simple, decision-ready signals, not elaborate visualisations. Whether this improves operations still has to be tested.
Language models and text analysisemerging
Research share +180% in 3 years · 11,876 papers in 2025
What it is about. The fastest-growing area of research on language models: how they find information, answer questions and behave in conversation.
ER-RAG: Enhance RAG with ER-Based Unified Modeling of Heterogeneous Data Source
ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data · 26 October  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Yikuan Xia and 10 others · Peking University, Huawei Technologies (China) · among the authors Bo Bob Bai, h-index 35
CONTEXTTo answer reliably, a chatbot can first look up documents and data and then reply from them (RAG). Often the information is scattered across web pages, databases and other sources, each needing its own search tool.
WHAT THEY DOA single, uniform way of querying all sources, inspired by the classic way databases describe things and the links between them. The system first picks the best sources, then builds the queries.
RESULTWith a relatively small model (8 billion parameters) it performs about as well as commercial systems using the most advanced models; it beats other mixed-source methods by 3.1% on an AI-judged score and searches 5.5 times faster.
WHY IT MATTERSGetting good answers from company data without the largest models means lower costs and data that can stay in-house.
Image generationemerging
Research share +130% in 3 years · 5,756 papers in 2025
What it is about. AI that creates or edits images, from photo retouching to generating pictures from a description.
Inst-Inpaint: Instructing to Remove Objects with Diffusion Models
International Journal of Computer Vision · 26 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Ahmet Burak Yildirim and 4 others · Bilkent University, Hacettepe University, Koç University (Türkiye) · among the authors Aykut Erdem, h-index 29
WHAT THEY DOTo erase an object from a photo you usually have to outline it by hand. Here you just write an instruction such as 'remove the dog on the left', and the system finds the object, deletes it and fills the gap realistically. They also release a dataset and the code.
WHY IT MATTERSPhoto editing by plain language becomes accessible to anyone; the abstract reports clear improvements but no figures.
RADAR OF THE DAY · LLMS AND GENERATIVE AI
What it is about. Large language models are the AIs behind chatbots; generative AI also creates images, audio and video. Today the focus is shifting to 'agents', AIs that carry out tasks by themselves, and to how to keep them under control.

(year on year)
«llm guardrails»▲ +2,712%▲ +6%
«ai governance»▲ +1,134%▲ +103%
«ai agent»▲ +364%▲ +130%
«local llm»▲ +498%▲ +52%
«retrieval augmented generation»▲ +87%▼ −83%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (few for guardrails, 17, and RAG, 3). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views for 'Large language model' −8%, RAG +9%, AI safety +12%; 'Model Context Protocol' had about 506,000 views (less than two years of history). Data updated 27 October.
In short: Developers are now building above all the tools to control AI: guardrails and governance grow far faster than everything else, and agents dominate the discussion. Plain RAG is becoming routine: still growing on GitHub, but barely discussed.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Explainable AI — AI that shows why it gave an answer, for example by highlighting the parts of an image it relied on.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) — a chatbot that first looks things up in documents or databases and then answers from what it found, like a student allowed to check the textbook.
Guardrails — rules and filters around an AI that block unwanted answers or actions, like the barriers along a mountain road.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on cybersecurity. Worth watching: the jump in projects on guardrails and governance suggests that controlling AI is becoming a product in its own right.

Several results today come from benchmarks and surveys, not from real-world use. A journal's quality does not guarantee that results are correct.
